summary.text: Interference happens when two coherent waves combine, adding their displacements while taking their phase difference into account.
Waves that are in step make a bigger wave, called constructive interference, while a crest meeting a trough makes a smaller one, called destructive interference.
It occurs with all kinds of waves, and light examples include the double-slit experiment, anti-reflective coatings and interferometers.

facts.label: Constructive when
facts.value: Phase difference is an even multiple of π

facts.label: Destructive when
facts.value: Phase difference is an odd multiple of π

facts.label: Cancelled energy
facts.value: Redistributed to other areas, not destroyed

facts.label: Fringe spacing
facts.value: Grows with longer wavelength and smaller crossing angle

items.prompt: Two stones hit a still pond at different spots. Where the two ripples meet crest to trough, what does the water do?

options.label: It rises to double height
It spins in a small whirlpool
It stays still, with no net displacement
It ripples faster than before

items.explain: Where the waves are in anti-phase their displacements cancel, leaving stationary lines on the surface.

items.prompt: Where does a wave's energy go at a spot where destructive interference cancels it out?

options.label: It is destroyed at that spot
It is redistributed to other areas
It is stored there until the waves end
It is turned into heat at that spot

items.explain: In ideal mediums energy is conserved, so cancellation at some points means the energy ends up elsewhere.

items.prompt: Two identical speakers play the same tone. At one spot, one sound wave arrives exactly half a cycle behind the other. What do you hear there?

options.label: A louder tone
A higher pitch
A doubled echo
Close to silence

items.explain: A phase difference of an odd multiple of π (180°) gives destructive interference, so equal waves cancel.

items.prompt: Two plane waves cross at a fixed angle. You switch to light with a longer wavelength. What happens to the fringes?

options.label: They get closer together
They spread farther apart
They stay exactly the same
They fade out completely

items.explain: The fringe spacing increases as the wavelength increases.

items.prompt: Two waves of the same type reach the same point. How is the resulting amplitude found?

options.label: By adding the individual amplitudes as a vector sum
By keeping only the stronger wave
By averaging the two amplitudes
By multiplying the two amplitudes

items.explain: The principle of superposition says the resultant amplitude is the vector sum of the individual amplitudes.

items.prompt: Water waves can be watched adding up. Why is light different when we study its interference?

options.label: Light beams never add up, so they cannot interfere at all
Light moves far too fast for any instrument to ever detect it
It only shows up when laser light sources are used for it
We never observe the fields adding directly; superposition is assumed to explain results

items.explain: Superposition of the electromagnetic field is an assumed phenomenon needed to explain how two beams pass through each other and continue on.

paragraphs.heading: Waves adding up
paragraphs.text: Interference is what happens when two coherent waves combine. Their displacements or intensities add, taking into account the difference in their phase. If the waves are in phase, the result has a larger amplitude, and this is called constructive interference. If they are out of phase, the result is smaller, and this is called destructive interference. Any type of wave can interfere, including light, radio, sound, water waves and matter waves.

paragraphs.heading: Crests and troughs
paragraphs.text: The rule underneath is the principle of superposition. When waves of the same type reach the same point, the amplitude there is the vector sum of their separate amplitudes. If a crest meets a crest of another wave with the same frequency, the amplitudes add. If a crest meets a trough, the result is the difference between them. In near-ideal media such as water and air, energy is conserved: where waves cancel, the energy moves to other areas.

paragraphs.heading: Stones in a pond
paragraphs.text: Picture two identical stones dropped into a still pool at different spots. Each sends out a circular wave. Where the two waves overlap, the net displacement at any point is the sum of the two. In some places the waves are in phase and the water moves the most; in others they are in anti-phase and there is no net movement at all. Those still parts of the surface form lines radiating out from the centre. The waves keep going, and only when they reach the shore is their energy absorbed.

paragraphs.heading: Phase in numbers
paragraphs.text: Constructive interference happens when the phase difference is an even multiple of π (180°), and destructive interference when it is an odd multiple. A phase difference in between gives a result between the minimum and the maximum. In symbols, one wave is W₁(x, t) = Acos (kx − ωt) and a second, shifted by a phase φ, is W₂(x, t) = Acos (kx − ωt + φ). Adding them and using a trigonometric identity for the sum of two cosines gives a single wave of the original frequency, moving the same way, with an amplitude of 2Acos (φ/2), so it grows and shrinks with the cosine of φ/2.

paragraphs.heading: Light is a special case
paragraphs.text: With light, we can never see the superposition of the electromagnetic field directly, the way we can with water. It is assumed, and it is needed to account for how two light beams cross and carry on along their own paths. Well-known examples of light interference include laser speckle, interferometers, anti-reflective coatings and the double-slit experiment. Interference only appears when the phase differences between the waves stay constant over the time you observe them. Quantum matter waves interfere as well.

paragraphs.heading: Making waves cancel
paragraphs.text: Sometimes the goal is for several waves with matching frequency and amplitude to add up to zero. This is the principle behind 3-phase power and the diffraction grating, and in both the result comes from spacing the phases evenly. A set of waves with equal amplitudes cancels when their phases are spaced equally in angle. A diffraction grating can be thought of as an interferometer with many beams. The Fabry–Pérot interferometer instead uses interference between many reflections.
